name: QUANTUM Trails
description: Step beyond the visible and into the world of QUANTUM. Join our Mediators, Ashi and Manasvi, as they trace the connections between science, art and imagination. Discover the stories and ideas behind the works and experience the many strange, playful and thought-provoking ways quantum phenomena come to life.

name: Meow Street Mystery
description:
We, the Three, of 13, Meow Street, host this treasure hunt and call upon your aid! O brave, capable and well-dressed strangers, might you find it in your hearts to follow the trail of our lost cat? 

Pass the trials of tricks, in this maze of mysteries, to perhaps find treasures and treats. Might you, bedecked in imaginative quantum garb, at once Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde or the Cheshire Cat alike, be the ones to band together and untangle this cat's cradle?

name: The Universe in a Nutshell: From Big Bang to Dark Energy
description:
In this talk, Rajeev Kumar will take you through the 14 billion years of the evolution of the Universe, from its earliest moments to the present epoch. From the tiny primordial fluctuations that seeded cosmic structures to the mysterious nature of dark matter and dark energy, our Universe presents a remarkable puzzle: why does it have the properties we observe? 

While the standard cosmological model describes a wealth of observations with remarkable success, the fundamental origins of these properties remain elusive. In this talk, I will explore how early Universe physics, primordial black holes, gravitational waves, and cosmic microwave background observations can uncover the physics underlying our cosmic history.

name: Optogenetics: Controlling Brain Cells with Light
description:
The 2026 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine went to researchers Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work on optogenetics. Optogenetics is the technique of using genetically expressed light-sensitive  proteins to control the activity of brain cells. 

Join Upinder Singh Bhalla for a lecture tracing the story of how very basic research into the light responsiveness of a single-celled plant micro-organism led to the discovery of light-sensitive proteins that allow current to flow into a cell. Learn how this was then developed into a powerful tool for studying the brain, and possibly for therapeutic purposes in the future. Come discover the path of development of optogenetics, both as a triumph of basic science, and also as a way to tell the story of many people who contributed fundamentally but were left aside when the prizes rolled in.

This lecture is organised in collaboration with Infosys Science Foundation.
